_comment: THE per-lesson hardware table. This file is the single source of truth: Terraform reads it
with jsondecode(), and infra/lib.sh reads it with jq. JSON rather than .tfvars precisely so
both can read the same bytes — a generated second copy is how the two drift apart.
kind is 'vm' (a Scaleway VM, console: Compute -> CPU & GPU Instances) or 'baremetal'
(Scaleway Elastic Metal, console: Bare Metal -> Elastic Metal). It is a per-lesson decision.
Lessons 1-5 all run on VMs, and that is a MEASURED choice rather than a cost optimisation.
Measured 2026-08-06 on this account, running the repo's own substrates and lessons unmodified:
* lesson 1's full scorecard is row-for-row identical on a VM and on EM-A116X-SSD metal
(all 17 findings, same BLOCKED/REACHED); rootless podman reports Rootless:true; runsc
reports 4.19.0-gvisor; the distro hardening the lessons lean on is the same
(unprivileged_bpf_disabled=2, perf_event_paranoid=4, kptr_restrict=1).
* a VM exposes /dev/kvm AND /dev/vhost-vsock (AMD EPYC 7543, svm, kvm_amd.nested=1), so
Kata boots a real guest — kernel 6.18.35, the same guest kernel the metal box recorded,
and lesson 4's surprise reproduces (guest unprivileged_bpf_disabled=0 vs node 2).
* lesson 5's NAT guest boots on a VM and takes a private primary address on its
default-route interface (192.168.122.0/24) — which is the whole point of that topology.
The older 'the guest must be L1, so lesson 5 needs metal' note was wrong: that symptom
(grub loads, kernel resets forever) was later traced to BIOS-vs-UEFI and seen on metal
too, which is why 50-nat-vm.sh passes --boot uefi.
What VMs buy, in order of how much it matters: Elastic Metal has a default quota of 2 on a
new organization, so four metal lessons could not be up at once and the reader had to run
them in batches; metal stock is per-offer and moves; and a metal OS install takes 10-15
minutes per box against under a minute for a VM. The money is a rounding error either way.
root_volume_gb is NOT a default worth trusting: a Scaleway VM's default root volume is 8 GB
usable and the Kata stack (nerdctl-full + kata-static) needs 9.3 GB. Metal's large local SSD
hid that, and the failure is a tar dying with 'No space left on device' mid-install.
ONE SHARED BOX PER CHAPTER (2026-08-13). Chapter 2 (lessons 2-4) shares `chapter-02-host` and
chapter 3 (lessons 6-9) shares `chapter-03-k8s`, each carrying every one of its chapter's
substrates at once. A shared lesson carries `box` instead of hardware, and `box` is the ONLY
indirection in this file: lib.sh's lesson_box() resolves it, everything else keeps reading the
row it lands on. The point is not money — several small short-lived boxes cost about what one
bigger one does. It is that each chapter's claim is `one machine, one flag selects between
boundaries`, and on a box carrying only gVisor the `runtimeClassName: gvisor` in lesson 7 (or
lesson 3's `--runtime runsc`) is a choice from a menu of one. On the shared box the other
runtimes are installed and provably working beside it, so the flag is doing what the chapter
says it does. check.sh proves that at provision time: it dispatches per substrate, so a
five-substrate entry fires all five boundary assertions against the one machine before any
lesson runs. The one exception is lesson 5, pinned to its own box by OpenShell's
private-primary-address requirement — the constraint is spelled out in chapter-02-host's `why`.
The honest cost: running ONE shared lesson now installs its whole chapter's substrates (~30 min
rather than ~8), because the menu is the point. infra/chapter-02.sh and infra/chapter-03.sh
amortize it over each chapter and still destroy every box on an EXIT trap, so no teardown
becomes a human's to remember.
Chapter 3 runs single-node k3s ON a disposable VM rather than against a
managed cluster (Scaleway Kapsule) or a nested one (minikube, kind). Three reasons, in order of
how much they matter:
* every boundary in the chapter is installed AT NODE LEVEL — runsc's binaries and a containerd
runtime, kata-static plus /dev/kvm, the OpenShell gateway. Managed node pools reconcile that
away, and minikube's docker driver nests the node inside a container, which breaks Kata and
makes lesson 6's 'the pod runs on the node's kernel' claim untrue of the thing you ran.
* a managed cluster hands you a kubeconfig, and a kubeconfig is a CREDENTIAL. k3s writes its
own on the box and it never leaves, so nothing has to be kept out of the repo by hand.
* k3s costs ~1.2 GB idle and 30-60 seconds, against 4-6 minutes to create a Kapsule cluster
whose nodes are billed at these very same VM prices. There is no money in it, only delay.
k3s enforces NetworkPolicy through an embedded kube-router controller (flannel alone does not),
which lesson 6 depends on — and which 60-k8s.sh ASSERTS rather than assumes, because a CNI that
accepts a NetworkPolicy object and silently ignores it is this repo's characteristic failure.
Prices are read live from the Scaleway catalogue by lib.sh — never hardcoded here, because a
stale price in a cost warning is worse than no price.

lesson-01-no-sandbox.why: The bare box IS the lesson. No engine, no runtime — the rogue agent runs as an ordinary host process, which is only acceptable on a machine that is destroyed minutes later.

chapter-02-host.why: NOT a lesson — the one host lessons 2, 3 and 4 share. It carries the chapter's host-side boundaries side by side — podman with crun as the untouched default (10), runsc as an opt-in podman runtime (20), containerd + kata-static for kata-qemu (30), and the devmapper snapshotter that makes kata-fc real (35) — so each lesson measures its own boundary on a machine where the alternatives are installed and provably working beside it, the same argument chapter-03-k8s makes for the runtimeClassName menu. check.sh fires all four assertions at provision time. ORDER 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 35: 20's smoke test needs podman installed, and 35 restarts containerd so it must follow 30. Nothing here has chapter 3's revert-on-restart trap — kata-static is files on disk, not a DaemonSet that undoes itself. WHY LESSON 5 IS NOT HERE: OpenShell's rootless-podman driver needs a genuinely private PRIMARY address on the default-route interface, which no Scaleway box has — so its box builds a Debian-13 NAT guest (50-nat-vm) and up.sh re-points the box's .state at that guest, terminally, after which every ssh and rsync for the box lands inside the guest. Host-level lessons cannot ride along on a box that has been relocated like that, so lesson 5 keeps its own; see its `why` and substrates/README.md. PRO2-XS (4 vCPU / 16 GB) because no NAT guest lives here, so the 2 GB Kata guest and the containerd/buildkit stack fit with headroom — a type purchasable since the account's identity verification lifted the quota that had pinned everything above PLAY2-MICRO at 0/0. 60 GB because the Kata stack measured 9.3 GB and 35 adds a 20 GB thin-pool data file plus 2 GB of metadata beside it: SPARSE and thin-provisioned, so a ceiling rather than disk spent, but the volume has to be able to honour it.

lesson-02-container.why: Runs on the shared chapter-2 host. Rootless podman on the host's own kernel — the rung every later boundary is measured against. The unprivileged `agent` user is created by cloud-init and is load-bearing: rootless is the claim this lesson makes, and a Scaleway VM otherwise logs in as root. The default runtime stays crun on a host where runsc and Kata are installed beside it (20-runsc registers gVisor strictly opt-in), so the baseline is a deliberate abstention from the menu rather than the only thing installed.

lesson-03-container-gvisor.why: Runs on the shared chapter-2 host. `--runtime runsc` chosen from a menu that also holds crun and Kata — the same one-flag selection lesson 7 makes with runtimeClassName, which is only meaningful because the alternatives answer beside it. runsc is user-space and needs no hardware feature; registered as an opt-in podman runtime so the default stays crun and Part 3 can re-run the previous rung on the same box.

lesson-04-container-kata.why: Runs on the shared chapter-2 host, whose /dev/kvm and /dev/vhost-vsock it needs. `--runtime io.containerd.kata.v2` boots a real guest kernel on the same machine where podman's crun and gVisor's runsc are working rungs, and 35 gives the same runtime a SECOND hypervisor (Firecracker), which needs the devmapper snapshotter because Firecracker has virtio-block and no virtio-fs — the container rootfs has to arrive as a block device. Read from inside, that is the whole difference: rootfs=virtiofs under kata-qemu, rootfs=ext4 under kata-fc.

lesson-05-container-openshell.why: OpenShell's rootless-podman driver refuses to start when the host's default-route address is public, and every Scaleway box has one. 50-nat-vm builds a libvirt guest on virbr0 whose primary address is private; the lesson then runs INSIDE that guest, reached through this box. Needs /dev/kvm for the guest and disk for its image.

chapter-03-k8s.why: NOT a lesson — the k3s cluster lessons 6, 7, 8 and 9 all share. It carries the four boundaries a workload selects with `runtimeClassName` (none / gvisor / kata-qemu / kata-fc) so that field is a real choice from a menu rather than the only runtime installed: measured 2026-08-13, one node served kernel 6.8.0-106-generic to a plain pod, 4.19.0-gvisor to a gVisor pod and guest 6.18.35 to a Kata pod, and installing Kata did NOT make it the default. 75 adds the devmapper snapshotter, which is what makes `kata-fc` — a class kata-deploy has always registered here and which has never worked — actually run: Firecracker has virtio-block and no virtio-fs, so a container rootfs must arrive as a BLOCK device, and without the snapshotter a kata-fc pod dies at sandbox creation with `snapshotter must be provided to unpack`. It configures no per-runtime snapshotter and must not: kata-deploy already writes `snapshotter = "devmapper"` on kata-fc and on nothing else, so kata-qemu stays on overlayfs and the split comes free and correct from upstream. ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING and it is about restarts, not files: 70 and 75 both run `systemctl restart k3s`, and nothing may restart k3s after 80, because a restart terminates the kata-deploy DaemonSet pod and that pod reverts its own install on termination. 75 sits between them for exactly that reason — loading a snapshotter needs containerd restarted, k3s embeds containerd, and there is no post-80 seam to do it in. 90 runs LAST and must not restart k3s — and it does not: it touches only `systemctl --user` openshell services, so kata-deploy survives it, which check.sh proves by booting a Kata guest after every substrate has run. 80 GB (up from 60) for 75's 25 GB thin-pool data file plus 2 GB of metadata; both are SPARSE and thin-provisioned, so that is a ceiling rather than disk spent — the OpenShell gateway image adds little beside it. LESSON 9 SHARES THIS NODE since 2026-08-13: the account's identity verification lifted the quota that had pinned every type above PLAY2-MICRO at 0/0, which was the only reason it sat on its own box. PRO2-S (8 vCPU / 32 GB) carries the resident OpenShell gateway and agent-sandbox controller beside lesson 8's Part 3b — repeated Kata guest boots — without the OOM that took the 8 GB node down.

lesson-06-k8s.why: Runs on the shared cluster. The plain Pod rung: no runtimeClassName at all, which on a cluster where gvisor and kata-qemu are both registered is a deliberate abstention rather than an absence — kata-deploy does not make Kata the default, so 'the pod runs on the NODE kernel' stays literally true of the thing you ran, and check.sh asserts exactly that before any lesson starts.

lesson-07-k8s-gvisor.why: Runs on the shared cluster. `runtimeClassName: gvisor` selected from a menu that also holds kata-qemu — which is the whole reason the field exists and the reason this lesson stopped being a box with one runtime on it.

lesson-08-k8s-kata.why: Runs on the shared cluster. Reads the RuntimeClass list rather than hardcoding a name (kata-deploy registers ~25 and the set moves between releases), then picks kata-qemu — a selection that is only meaningful because gvisor is sitting in the same list.

lesson-09-k8s-openshell.why: Runs on the shared cluster. OpenShell is the one chapter-3 boundary NOT selected with `runtimeClassName` — its sandbox pods take their runtime class from the GATEWAY, because `openshell sandbox create` has no such flag — but it is installed on the same node, so the audit/policy axis is measured beside the runtime menu it composes with rather than on different hardware. It shares since 2026-08-13: identity verification lifted the quota that had forced it onto its own 8 GB box, and PRO2-S (32 GB) holds its resident gateway and agent-sandbox controller beside lesson 8's repeated Kata boots — see chapter-03-k8s's `why`. Note what is NOT here: lesson 5's 50-nat-vm. The public-default-route constraint belongs to OpenShell's rootless-podman driver, and the kubernetes driver's sandbox callback is an in-cluster Service on a private ClusterIP.

lesson-16-compose-gvisor-openshell.why: Runs on the shared cluster. The COMPOSITION lesson, and the tutorial's one place gVisor+OpenShell has a mechanism: OpenShell's kubernetes driver selects the lower runtime per sandbox with a driver-config overlay that lands as the pod's `runtimeClassName: gvisor`. It reuses lesson 9's policy byte-for-byte and swaps only the runtime underneath, so any row that moves moved because of gVisor. The finding is a FAILURE MODE, and measured on OpenShell 0.0.99 a subtle one: gVisor answers ENOSYS to landlock(), so the filesystem clause silently LOSES its Landlock backing (a HIGH `landlock-unavailable` audit finding) — but `fs_policy_write` stays BLOCKED, because this driver also backs the read-only paths with a read-only ROOT FILESYSTEM. So the lost layer is MASKED: the attack outcome matches the safe Kata stack and the audit trail is the only witness. policy-hard.yaml (hard_requirement) makes it fail closed (refuse to start). Asserts `runtimeClassName` from the pod AND the 4.19.0-gvisor kernel from inside — never the flag. THE NEVER-RUN COMBO: reproduced on a live box 2026-08-14, and the prior-art's predicted `flips to ALLOWED` did NOT hold on this OpenShell version — reported, not faked. Chapter 2 cannot host this (rootless podman cannot drive runsc, lesson 14) and chapter 4 cannot (gVisor unsupported on OpenShift, lesson 18). NO OWN HARDWARE ROW — it shares chapter-03-k8s, which already carries gVisor beside runc and Kata.

lesson-17-compose-kata-openshell.why: Runs on the shared cluster. The positive half of lesson 16's finding: the SAME OpenShell policy stacked on Kata (`runtimeClassName: kata-qemu`) instead of gVisor, where it HOLDS — `fs_policy_write` stays blocked because a real guest kernel ships Landlock and OpenShell's landlock() call succeeds inside the VM. Part 2 shows hard_requirement STARTS here (the requirement is satisfiable), the mirror of lesson 16's refuse-to-start. Asserts Kata engaged from inside by a guest kernel that DIFFERS from the node's (on k3s it does; lesson 19 on OpenShift must use DMI because there it matches). Same driver-config overlay mechanism as lesson 16, same shared box, so the two compositions are measured on identical hardware one flag apart.

lesson-19-compose-kata-openshell.why: Runs on the shared SNO cluster, like lessons 10-13: its run.sh neither provisions nor destroys (the €0.263/hr box is human-owned; teardown is infra/down.sh openshift-sno). The COMPOSITION on the platform it is sold on — OpenShell over Kata, where Kata is the sandboxed-containers OPERATOR (RuntimeClass `kata`, one class not k3s's 25, per lesson 12) and OpenShell must clear SCC admission (the privileged grant lesson 11 sets up and lesson 13 pays). Selects the runtime with the same driver-config overlay as lessons 16/17 (`runtimeClassName: kata`). Expect fs_policy_write BLOCKED (the operator's guest ships Landlock, so lesson 16's gVisor regression does NOT happen), and assert the VM from INSIDE by DMI=KVM/virtio, never the kernel string — Red Hat builds the guest kernel from the same RHEL base so it matches the node (Trap #12). Same stock ubi9 image and oc-cp suite delivery as lesson 13, because RHCOS has no registry to bake an image into.

openshift-sno.why: NOT a lesson — it is the single-node OpenShift CLUSTER that chapter 4's lessons (10-13 and the composition leaf 19) all share. One entry rather than four, because installing SNO takes far longer than a lesson does and re-installing it four times would be absurd. It lives in this table so Terraform owns it and `down.sh --all` sweeps it: at EUR 0.263/hr, forgetting this box is the single most expensive mistake available in this repo. Metal is genuinely required here (Kata needs /dev/kvm AND cluster-admin on a real node); it is the ONLY place in the tutorial that is true. `substrates` is empty on purpose: the SNO install cannot run through up.sh's substrate model, because it REPLACES the operating system mid-flight — the box that finishes the install is RHCOS and has no `agent` user, no repo checkout and no uv. It is driven instead by infra/openshift-sno/install.sh, which runs on the workstation.
